Embarrassment can make a person avoid a fact until they are ready, which is closer to omission than to a lie.
People simplify for children or when in a hurry.
common_false_positives: A colleague gives a delivery date that then slips.
Someone says 'I'm fine' to get through a work day.
A friend remembers a name or place wrongly.
Two witnesses describe an event differently from where they stood.
discernment_questions: What do I actually know, from a record or a witness, as opposed to a feeling?
Could the speaker have believed it when they said it?
When the facts came out, was the account owned or did it change?
Is this one claim, or one of several that haven't held up?
Would I decide differently with the true version, and does it matter here?
less_concerning_if: The correction is offered without prompting when they realize.
The false detail has no bearing on your decisions.
Their other claims check out when you look.
more_concerning_if: The false claim shaped a big decision about money, health, someone's whereabouts or a legal matter.
Further claims keep failing when checked.
Owning it is followed by blaming you for checking.
pattern_over_time_signs: You start verifying small things you would once have accepted.
Corrections arrive only after you find the record yourself.
Explanations of earlier claims keep changing.
True statements from the same person start to be doubted as well, and sorting true from false becomes your job.
live_fields.repair_check: A plain correction names what was untrue and what it cost you, and information is then volunteered before you ask for it. An apology that spends most of its length on why you shouldn't have checked has repaired nothing.
live_fields.boundary_respect_check: If you say you need claims you can check, such as the receipt or the message, watch the next few weeks. Respect looks like being handed the document without a fight. Being told you are paranoid for asking suggests the request was not taken in.
live_fields.psychological_mechanism: People generally assume that what they are told is true, because checking everything is exhausting. A lie uses that default. Once it is discovered, trust tends to break wider than the lie itself, since the listener cannot easily tell which other statements were true. Rebuilding the picture takes effort, and some people stay watchful long afterwards.
live_fields.possible_impact_on_receiver: A sharp jolt on discovery comes first, then going back through past conversations to sort true from false. Believing is an ordinary default, yet many feel foolish for having done it. Others turn into checkers, and some find the relationship, or the institution, harder to rely on afterwards even when the lie was small.

response_options.soft_clarification: Lead with the fact rather than the accusation: 'The bank record shows the payment on the 14th. Help me understand what happened.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Say that on money and safety matters you need claims that can be checked. For example: 'On this kind of thing, I need to see the record, not just hear it.'
response_options.disengagement: Where the stakes are high, stop acting on this person's unverified claims. Decide using what you can check yourself, and let the rest wait.
response_options.support_seeking: Check your reading with someone neutral who can look at the documents. That way you are not relying on memory alone or on the other person's version.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, ask for important statements in writing and keep the record. If a false statement affected a decision, take the documents to a supervisor or HR rather than arguing the point out loud.

live_fields.boundary_script: "Being able to rely on what you tell me matters to me. When it's about money or plans, I'll ask to see the confirmation. That isn't an accusation, it's how I'm going to make decisions from now on."
live_fields.safety_note: Lying becomes safety-relevant when the false claims concern where someone is, or what has been done with your money or documents. It also does when asking about the truth is met with anger or threats. Keep copies of records you can verify, and if questions bring fear, speak to an advocate or lawyer before raising it again.
misuse_warning: Calling someone a liar when they may have been mistaken or remember differently closes the conversation. It also treats a guess about what they knew as fact.
Treating one inaccurate statement as proof that everything else the person says is false.
live_fields.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Lying by Omission says nothing false but leaves out the piece that would change your decision. A lie puts a false statement on the table. Fabricated Evidence adds a manufactured document or screenshot to back the claim, so there is a physical thing to examine. Exaggeration begins with something true and stretches it. A lie stands alone as a flat statement the speaker knows is untrue.

Information Cascades.definition: A belief spreading because it's safer to agree than question.

live_fields.expanded_definition: An information cascade happens when people set aside what they would conclude alone. They follow what the people before them seem to believe. Each person's acceptance becomes a signal to the next. The claim gains weight with every repeat, although no new evidence has been added. One shared opinion means little, and popular beliefs are often right. A cascade is likely when you trace the trail back and find people citing one another. There may be a single thin source at the bottom, or none. A cascade is also likely when asking for evidence draws more social chill than the claim deserves.
live_fields.why_this_matters: Someone can end up judged on a belief nobody actually checked. Correcting it means pushing against a whole group's momentum, instead of answering one person's claim. A reputation or rumor that has hardened this way can be very hard to undo.
what_it_is: A claim or reputation gains credibility from how many people appear to hold it, and no new evidence is added along the way.
Each later person treats earlier agreement as information. Anyone with doubts stays quiet because the early voices looked so sure.
You see it in office rumors about a coworker, neighborhood gossip, investment fads, product hype, and health scares that get passed around group chats.
Often resting on a first source that was thin, misread or never checked, which later citations make look solid.
Different from a staged campaign: nobody has to coordinate it, and everyone in the chain may be sincere.
what_it_is_not: A widely held belief that is simply correct. Popularity and truth overlap far more often than they split.
Relying on a source with a real track record, such as a physician or a reference book, instead of re-checking everything yourself.
Several people who each tested the claim in a different way and got the same result, like labs repeating a measurement.
One loud person repeating a claim, which is persuasion by a single voice and not a chain of followers.
A cautious group that says openly, "we are going by the expert's word", and can name the expert.
Someone changing their mind after hearing others' reasons. The marker here is people citing each other's numbers in place of anything independent.
this_may_be_it_when: Asked for the source, people name one another instead of a record, a test or a firsthand witness.
The trail back ends at one unchecked post, remark or secondhand story.
Confidence in the room is much higher than the amount of evidence anyone can produce.
People with doubts say afterward that they kept quiet because everyone else seemed certain.
A correction from a reliable source changes few minds, because the belief has become a group position.
this_may_not_be_it_when: Several people can describe how they checked it, using different methods.
The claim traces to a record, measurement or witness that you can examine yourself.
A question about the claim gets an answer instead of a cooler mood.
People in the group have changed their stance after seeing new evidence.
The belief is held by a handful of friends who each hold it for their own reasons.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Nobody has time to verify everything, so leaning on other people's judgment is how most knowledge travels.
A fast-moving warning, such as a road closure, can be accurate, and speed alone does not make it a cascade.
People repeat things they heard in good faith without ever claiming to have checked them.
common_false_positives: A scientific finding accepted widely after many teams repeated it and got the same answer.
A local rumor that proves true because several neighbors saw the event with their own eyes.
A team adopting a tool because a few members tried it and reported what happened.
discernment_questions: Can the claim be traced to something one person actually saw, measured or recorded?
If nobody else believed it, how much would the claim still persuade you?
When you ask where it came from, do you get a source or a change of mood?
Has anyone in the group said they doubted it and then stayed silent?
Does the original source, once found, say what everyone says it says?
less_concerning_if: The claim traces back to genuine, independent checking by more than one person.
People in the group welcome a request for the source and help you look.
The belief is low-stakes and nobody is being judged on it.
more_concerning_if: The belief is being used to exclude, report or penalize a named person.
The original source, once found, is thin, garbled or missing.
People who question it are called disloyal instead of answered.
pattern_over_time_signs: The same claim returns in the same words across different chats, tables or teams.
Corrections reach far fewer people than the original claim did.
A reputation sticks to someone even after the facts behind it have been shown to be wrong.
You find yourself passing the belief on without remembering where you picked it up.
live_fields.repair_check: Suppose the belief turns out wrong. Look at whether the people who passed it along can say where it came from and what they now know. Correcting the record in the same places the claim spread counts for something. Quietly dropping the subject while the reputation lingers leaves the damage in place.
live_fields.boundary_respect_check: After you ask where a claim came from, does the room produce a source, or does the mood turn toward you? Honest groups treat a source request as ordinary. A group that hears it as disloyalty is showing how little the belief rests on.
live_fields.psychological_mechanism: People often take other people's visible choices as information, especially when a topic is unfamiliar or being wrong would cost them socially. Once a few early voices agree, later people may set aside their own private doubts, and each added agreement makes speaking up cost more. The belief can feel settled long before anyone has examined it.
live_fields.possible_impact_on_receiver: Some are treated as guilty of something nobody can quite prove. Some start doubting their own reasonable questions, or go along with views they hold only loosely. Some feel shut out once they ask for a source. Someone carrying a hardened reputation may find that corrections reach fewer people than the original claim did.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask the person repeating it a plain question: "Where did you first see that?" Honest answers will usually point somewhere you can look.
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline to pass it on until you have found something firsthand: "I'm not going to share this until I've seen the original."
response_options.disengagement: Step out of a thread where the only proof offered is how many people agree. Come back after you have looked for the source yourself.
response_options.support_seeking: Take the claim to someone who knows the area, such as a librarian, a fact-checking service or a person who works in the field. Ask how it could be checked.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a rumor about a colleague is moving through the office, ask your manager or HR for the source. Do it one-to-one, before anyone acts on it in a review or decision.

live_fields.boundary_script: Verification script (to yourself, before repeating it): "Have I seen the evidence, or only seen that other people believe it? Who said it first, and would I still repeat it if nobody else had?"
live_fields.safety_note: A cascade is mostly a sourcing problem and not a danger. That changes when the belief becomes a reason to exclude, report or punish a named person. An example is a rumor of misconduct moving through a workplace or school. Then keep dated notes of what is being said and by whom. Take them to HR, a school counselor or a legal aid clinic before answering in the group.
misuse_warning: Calling a belief a cascade just because many people hold it dismisses beliefs that are widely held because they are true. The label needs a trail with nothing independent at the bottom.
Telling worried neighbors or coworkers they are "just following the crowd" skips the question of whether they happen to be right.
live_fields.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Strategic Ambiguity is vague wording that lets a speaker later claim different meanings. A cascade can run on perfectly clear statements that were simply never checked. Gatekeeping controls who gets information or access, but a cascade needs no controller, only people following people. In a cascade, agreement is the evidence.

Computational Propaganda.definition: Automated accounts, targeting and amplification software are used to make political messages look more popular or spontaneous than they are.

live_fields.expanded_definition: Computational Propaganda is political persuasion carried out with software. It uses automated accounts, networks of fake profiles and algorithm-boosted content that pass as ordinary people talking. It differs from a single troll or a loud real user. It relies on volume and coordination that no group of individuals could produce by hand. Parties and campaigns openly coordinate messaging and use scheduling tools, so automation alone is not the sign. Attribution is technical work, and a hard-arguing account is not evidence of a network.
live_fields.why_this_matters: The sense of what most people believe shapes what any one person feels able to say aloud. Here that sense gets set by accounts that are not people. Real voices can be outnumbered, and honest users get wrongly accused of being bots.
what_it_is: Political messages pushed through automated or fake accounts that imitate real, independent users.
A matter of scale and speed. The same message can appear thousands of times in minutes, which a crowd of real people rarely does.
Sometimes mixed with real users who are drawn in and share the content, which then spreads it further.
Seen on screens as patterns in accounts and timing, rather than in what any single post says.
Different from a hired commentator who writes under their own name, because the hallmark is simulated people.
what_it_is_not: Parties, campaigns and advocacy groups legitimately coordinating their messaging, which is ordinary politics.
Scheduling tools and staff-run accounts, which are not bots.
An account that argues aggressively or repeats a view often. Intensity is not proof of a network.
Many real people sharing a viral post for their own reasons.
A news organization's automated feed that is clearly labeled as automated.
this_may_be_it_when: Large numbers of accounts share very similar wording, timing and links, yet have no visible connection.
Account histories are short, blank or inconsistent with the persona they present.
Researchers or the platform itself have documented the network and removed it.
The activity spikes around a political event and disappears afterwards.
Accounts respond to criticism with the same stock replies rather than the content of your reply.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The only evidence is that someone disagrees with you strongly and often.
The accounts are real people who found the same post and shared it.
You have judged by a single profile feature, such as a missing photo.
Similar wording comes from a widely circulated news line.
You cannot see the account's history and are guessing from one post.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Many people copy a funny or striking phrase and spread it quickly without any coordination.
Shy or privacy-minded users keep sparse profiles and no photo.
Fans or supporters may organize openly in a group chat to post together. That is visible coordination, not a hidden one.
common_false_positives: A hashtag that trends because a real event drew millions of genuine reactions.
A brand or party running its own clearly labeled, scheduled posts.
An elderly relative who reposts the same chain message to everyone.
discernment_questions: Does this account have a history that predates the topic, with signs of a real life?
Is the pile-on built of accounts with nothing in common except the message?
Would I judge the claim differently if I knew only a few people were behind it?
Has a platform, researcher or journalist reported on this particular activity?
Am I calling this fake because the evidence shows it, or because I cannot believe so many people disagree?
less_concerning_if: The accounts are identifiable people or organizations who are open about their affiliations.
Spread of the message tracks real events and real conversations.
Independent researchers have looked and found ordinary activity.
more_concerning_if: Accounts posing as local citizens turn out to be run from elsewhere or by one operator.
Messaging targets real individuals with harassment or the spread of their personal details.
Platform or independent reports connect the activity to a concealed sponsor.
pattern_over_time_signs: Clusters of near-identical accounts reappear under new names after earlier ones are removed.
The same talking points rise and fall in step across unrelated topics.
Activity surges around elections or debates and falls sharply after.
You find your own feed shows one view as dominant while people you know offline hold a wider range.
live_fields.repair_check: Real correction means the operator is identified, the accounts are taken down, and a public explanation says what was automated and by whom. Quiet deletion followed by the same messages from new profiles leaves the network intact.
live_fields.boundary_respect_check: When you ask a suspicious account a genuine question about itself, does it engage with what you said, or fall back on stock lines? A real person can answer in their own words. Canned repetition, or silence followed by more of the same, is informative.
live_fields.psychological_mechanism: People often read the number of voices saying something as a sign of what is common and safe to think. A large, steady stream of apparently independent posts can make a view feel mainstream and can make dissenters feel isolated. Seeing the same claim many times also tends to make it feel more familiar and so more plausible.
live_fields.possible_impact_on_receiver: Seeing an apparently overwhelming majority can make a person doubt their own views. Others hold back from posting or feel anger at accounts that later turn out to be fake. Some grow suspicious of strangers online, honest ones included. Some start calling every opponent a bot, which damages real conversation.

response_options.soft_clarification: Before replying to a surprising account, check its profile and history. A single honest question such as 'Can you tell me more about how you came to this view?' shows whether anyone is there.
response_options.firm_boundary: Decide not to share or boost content from accounts you cannot verify as real people, however well it fits your opinions.
response_options.disengagement: Mute, block or leave a thread filled with identical replies, and avoid arguing with accounts that may not be people.
response_options.support_seeking: Report suspicious patterns, with links and dates, to the platform's reporting tool, a fact-checking group or a reporter who covers online influence.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If you work in communications, moderation or research, keep dated records of what you saw. Follow your organization's process for reporting suspected coordinated activity.

live_fields.boundary_script: "Is there a real person behind this? Does the account have a life that predates this topic? If only a handful of people were posting this, would I still believe so many agree, or am I counting accounts instead of people?"
live_fields.safety_note: Reading or being outnumbered by suspect accounts is not a physical danger. It would change if networks target a named person with harassment, threats or the spread of their address or workplace. If that happens, document everything, report it to the platform, and contact a lawyer, a support service or the police if you feel unsafe.
misuse_warning: Calling anyone who disagrees with you a 'bot' dismisses real people and ends conversations. The claim needs evidence about the account, and its opinions alone are not enough.
Public accusations against a named account can wrongly expose an ordinary person to harassment.
live_fields.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Astroturfing stages grassroots support by many means, including paid people and letters, while Computational Propaganda depends on software and fake accounts. Manufactured Consent shapes which real voices get coverage and needs no fake accounts. Wedge Issue Exploitation is about which divisive topic gets pushed, and bots are only one possible amplifier.

Post-Truth Epistemic Manipulation.made_of: Repetition as Truth + Gish Gallop / Firehose of Falsehood + False Consensus / Social Proof Pressure
Post-Truth Epistemic Manipulation.definition: Emotion and identity are made to count for more than evidence, so asking what is true starts to seem beside the point.

live_fields.expanded_definition: 'Post-truth' is a term for public life where appeals to emotion and identity count for more than facts you can check. As a manipulation pattern, it is a steady flood of contradictions, denials and 'who can really know' messages. People end up unsure whether anything can be verified. Doubting a specific claim is healthy. This pattern pushes doubt about whether claims can be tested at all. One dishonest statement, or one sincere moment of cynicism, does not show it. What marks it is the scale and the effect, which are fatigue and giving up.
live_fields.why_this_matters: When nothing can be known, nothing can be checked, and someone left doubting everything has no ground from which to object to anything. They may also fall back on whoever sounds most certain, or on their own group.
what_it_is: A climate of doubt about whether facts can be established, not a single false claim.
Works through volume and contradiction. There are many stories, denials and counter-stories, and sorting them takes more effort than most people have.
Can come from governments, parties, companies or influencers. Ordinary audiences can also repeat the mood themselves, so the source is rarely clear.
Often voiced as 'both sides are the same' or 'no one can really know'.
Different from honest skepticism, which still holds that claims can be tested and wants better tests.
what_it_is_not: Distrust of institutions is often earned. Saying that reporting has bias or uncertainty is honest. The difference is between doubting one claim and giving up on the idea that claims can be tested at all.
A scientist saying results are uncertain and giving the margin of error.
Reporters who correct their own mistakes in public.
Philosophical debate about knowledge, which is a serious subject and not a campaign.
Fatigue after a hard news cycle, when anyone may say 'I can't keep up'.
Healthy disagreement over what the evidence shows, with both sides citing evidence.
this_may_be_it_when: Disproved claims are replaced by new ones instead of being withdrawn, and the supply never stops.
Checking is treated as pointless or naive, regardless of what the check shows.
The message attacks the idea of verification itself, and goes beyond one fact.
Contradictory stories about one event flood in at once, and the confusion becomes the main result.
Real records and fake ones are treated by the speaker as equally untrustworthy.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The doubt is aimed at a specific claim and the speaker explains what evidence would settle it.
The skeptic accepts a result when the evidence is shown.
Sources disagree because the event is complex and new.
You feel worn out after heavy news, and the doubt fades with rest.
The criticism of a source gives concrete, checkable examples of past errors.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Past institutional failures give people real reasons to question official statements.
Fast news creates contradictory early reports, which is normal.
Many people say 'no one knows' as a way of staying humble about complex topics.
Algorithm-driven feeds serve conflicting content with no plan by anyone.
common_false_positives: A teacher who tells students to question every source and then shows how to check.
A friend venting 'I trust nothing now' after a scandal.
Researchers who disagree in print on a hard question.
A satirical show that mocks all sides.
discernment_questions: Am I doubting this particular claim, or have I begun to doubt that anything can be checked?
What would count as good evidence on this, and have I looked for it?
Is there anyone I trust to be right about something? Who, and why?
Who benefits when I stop checking?
Has the volume of conflicting stories left me too tired to sort them?
less_concerning_if: You can still name a few sources that have earned your trust, and say why.
Doubt leads you to look further rather than to stop.
more_concerning_if: You catch yourself saying nothing can be known and have stopped reading, voting or checking.
People around you treat the same record as proof or forgery depending on whose side it favors.
You are pushed to give up on facts and told to rely on one personality or group for the answers.
pattern_over_time_signs: Conflicting claims keep arriving, and few are settled before the next wave.
A growing share of conversations ends in 'you can't trust anything'.
People you know shift from 'I disagree' to 'it doesn't matter what's true'.
You notice yourself or others sharing without checking, because checking stopped seeming worth it.
live_fields.repair_check: Where trust is restored, sources publish their evidence, admit errors and let others check. A promise to be more honest next time, with no method others could test, restores very little.
live_fields.boundary_respect_check: Ask what evidence would change their mind, and listen to the answer. A concrete answer shows that claims can still be tested. 'Nothing would, they all lie' shows that the idea that testing is impossible is holding steady.
live_fields.psychological_mechanism: Faced with more contradictory claims than we can sort, many of us save effort. We switch off or retreat to the group we feel loyal to. Repeated falsehoods that carry no cost can teach that truth does not matter. Doubt can then spread from the false claim to the whole idea of checking.
live_fields.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe exhaustion, cynicism, a sense that the effort to find out is wasted, and withdrawal from news or civic life. Others describe leaning harder on one trusted voice or group because everything else feels unreliable. Some feel shame at having been fooled and stop trusting even honest sources.

response_options.soft_clarification: Separate the two doubts out loud: 'I doubt that claim, and here is what would settle it. I do not doubt that things can be checked.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline to accept 'everyone lies' as an answer. Ask for the specific claim and the specific evidence, and stay on that.
response_options.disengagement: Limit how much conflicting commentary you take in. Follow a few sources with a record of corrections, and check them less often but more carefully.
response_options.support_seeking: Talk to a librarian, a teacher or a friend who enjoys checking things, and practice tracing one claim from start to finish together.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: In a team, agree on how disputed facts will be settled: which records count, who can check them, and where corrections are posted.

live_fields.boundary_script: "I can doubt this one claim without doubting everything. What would settle it, who has checked it, and have I read the original? If I cannot tell, I will say I do not know instead of pretending I do."
live_fields.safety_note: Post-truth pressure is usually not a physical danger. It matters for safety when doubt about everything leads people to ignore real warnings, such as medical, weather or financial ones. If a decision touches your health, money or home, check with a doctor, an official emergency channel or a trusted professional. Do not rely on your feed alone.
misuse_warning: Calling a person's honest doubt 'post-truth' can be used to shut down legitimate criticism of institutions.
If you use the label for views you simply disagree with, it stops describing a method. It becomes a way of saying your opponents do not care about facts.
live_fields.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Manufactured Consent tries to install an agreement. This pattern tries to wear away the shared ground on which agreement or disagreement is judged. Computational Propaganda names the automated machinery that can flood a feed. Post-truth manipulation names the climate of doubt that results. Overton Window Manipulation moves what is acceptable to say, not what can be known. The difference is the target, which is the possibility of knowing at all.

Honey Trapping.made_of: Manufactured Intimacy -> Shared Secret Binding -> Blackmail / Leverage Exploitation
Honey Trapping.definition: An apparent romance or sexual relationship is the route by which access, information or leverage is obtained from you.

live_fields.expanded_definition: Honey trapping is the use of an apparent romance or sexual relationship as the means of an intelligence operation. The affection is the delivery method, and the goal sits behind it. It appears in espionage history and counterintelligence training, and it is rare compared with ordinary dating. From the inside it looks like a normal relationship, so one odd detail proves nothing. What matters is a combination of three things: sensitive access, a relationship that moves faster than the facts support, and later pressure.
live_fields.why_this_matters: The relationship itself was the tool. So finding out means losing the connection and facing the results of everything shared inside it, all at the same moment. Shame and fear of exposure can keep people silent, even when telling a security officer early would limit the damage.
what_it_is: A relationship that is real in feeling for the person targeted but staged in purpose for the other side.
Mostly discussed in connection with people who hold sensitive jobs, clearances, or access to information others want.
Often involves closeness that later turns into requests or pressure, rather than a single moment.
A romance scam is a separate pattern. A stranger online builds affection to ask an ordinary person for money, and no access or secrets are involved.
Usually visible only in hindsight, once the pieces are laid side by side.
what_it_is_not: Relationships involving people in sensitive positions are overwhelmingly just relationships. Suspicion about a partner's motives is not evidence of an operation.
Attraction between colleagues, conference-goers, or neighbors, which happens constantly without anything being arranged.
A partner who is curious about your day, including your job, because they care about you.
A romance scam, where a stranger online builds affection to ask for money. It hurts, but it is a different pattern.
A partner who is private about their past or family for reasons of shame, grief, or safety.
Ordinary jealousy or secrecy in a relationship, which says nothing about espionage.
this_may_be_it_when: You hold a role with real access, and a close relationship formed unusually fast around the time you gained it.
The partner's questions keep steering toward specifics that matter to outsiders, such as names, systems, or schedules.
Basic facts about them do not hold up when you gently check, such as where they work or who they know.
Intimate photos, recordings, or messages are mentioned as something that could be shared, even as a joke.
A friend, security officer, or employer's guidance has told you to report contacts of this kind, and the new partner fits.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They know your friends and family, and your circle has met them over time.
Their questions about work are general and fade when you say you cannot discuss it.
The relationship's speed matches how you both usually date.
Their life checks out through ordinary means, such as a known employer and shared acquaintances.
Nothing has ever been requested, hinted at, or held over you.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Two people in the same field meet often because their jobs overlap.
Intense early romance is common and is driven by novelty and hope.
A new partner may ask about work because it is simply a large part of your life.
common_false_positives: A partner who works for a competitor or a rival organization, and who met you openly through the industry.
A partner who stays vague about money or family because of an unrelated private difficulty.
The anxiety of a person with a clearance who begins to wonder about every new date.
discernment_questions: Can people in my own life confirm that this person is who they say they are?
Did their interest in my work come before or after I mentioned what I do?
Has any sexual or private material been referred to as something that could be used?
Does my workplace have a duty or a person to whom contacts like this can be reported without penalty?
Am I asking these questions because of something I saw, or only because I am anxious?
less_concerning_if: You feel free to talk to others about the relationship.
more_concerning_if: Intimate material is mentioned as a way to pressure you, even indirectly.
The person begins to ask for favors tied to your access, framed as proof of caring.
They discourage you from telling colleagues or friends about the relationship.
pattern_over_time_signs: The balance of questions shifts from you to your job.
People who might check on the relationship are kept away from it.
Warmth rises and falls with how much you share or provide.
You start hiding things from your own workplace to protect the relationship.
live_fields.repair_check: If you raise concerns, a genuine partner can accept being checked. They introduce friends, answer plain questions, and do not bristle at your employer's rules. What only looks like repair is more intensity, new promises, or a tearful appeal that you trust them.
live_fields.boundary_respect_check: Watch how they react when you say you will not discuss work. Do they let it go and ask about something else? Or does affection cool, or pressure rise? The reaction to a closed door is more telling than any single question.
live_fields.psychological_mechanism: Closeness can lower a person's guard. Sexual or romantic attachment can make someone want to please a partner and hide anything that might spoil it. Shared secrets can create a sense of obligation. Later, embarrassment and fear of exposure can make a person comply or stay quiet rather than report, which keeps the situation going.
live_fields.possible_impact_on_receiver: The loss lands twice. The relationship they believed in turns out to have been something else, and there may be professional consequences for what was shared. Many report shame, anger at themselves, and a fear of telling anyone. Some pull away from friends because of the embarrassment.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask a plain, calm question about something checkable, such as 'Can I meet your coworkers or friends sometime?' Then notice how it is received.
response_options.firm_boundary: Keep work details out of the relationship altogether. You could say: 'I do not discuss work with anyone, including people I love.' Say it the same way every time.
response_options.disengagement: Pause sharing anything sensitive while you check things out, and keep your conversations about everyday life.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell a trusted friend what has been happening, and consider a lawyer or counselor, so you are not holding it alone.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If your job has a security office or a reporting process for unusual contacts, it is usually better to go early than to wait. Early reports usually leave you more options.

live_fields.boundary_script: "I keep my work separate from my relationships, with everyone, and that won't change. I'm happy to talk about anything else."
live_fields.safety_note: Watch for any mention of private photos, recordings or messages being shared. Watch too for pressure that grows once you have shared something. Do not handle it alone. A lawyer, the security or legal contact at your workplace, or a trusted person can help you plan the next step. Do this before anything is disclosed.
misuse_warning: Accusing a partner of being an operative on thin evidence can wreck a real relationship. It can also bring harassment down on an innocent person.
Using the label to explain away any breakup or betrayal turns a rare category into a catch-all.
live_fields.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Agent of Influence Operations uses public figures who speak to an audience. Honey trapping happens in private, through one person's intimate trust. MICE Framework Exploitation is the analyst's checklist of levers such as money or compromise, and honey trapping is one route to the compromise lever. Strategic Deception misleads whole adversaries. Here, one person is deceived about a single relationship.

Strategic Deception (Denial & Deception.definition: Real facts are kept hidden while a false picture is put on display in their place.

live_fields.expanded_definition: The title joins two related behaviors that are usually discussed together. Denial means keeping the real thing out of view: concealing a capability, a plan, or a site. Deception means putting a false picture in its place so others believe it. They are two sides of one effort, and the pairing is used in security studies. It happens at the scale of states, armies and large organizations. Ordinary secrecy is not the same: not being told something differs from being pointed the wrong way.
live_fields.why_this_matters: Plans get laid against a picture of the world that was arranged to be believed. The error usually shows only when acting on it can no longer be undone. For the public, it also means official accounts and leaked ones both deserve a second look.
what_it_is: Two linked parts: denial hides the real thing, and deception supplies a false substitute. Describing either alone misses the combination.
Done by states, militaries, and large institutions across several channels at once, not by individuals.
Aimed at what an opponent believes about intentions, capabilities, plans or timing.
Historians and analysts judge it in hindsight, usually from released records, because it is meant to be invisible while it works.
Different from simple secrecy, which keeps something quiet without installing a false belief.
what_it_is_not: Ordinary secrecy is legitimate; institutions and states keep capabilities and intentions confidential without staging a coordinated illusion.
Not being told something is not the same as being actively pointed the wrong way.
An honest mistake or a failure of intelligence analysis, which can look the same from outside.
Ordinary public relations, spin, or a company's carefully worded statement.
A rumor that turns out false, without a coordinating hand behind it.
Bluffing in a negotiation or game, which is limited and understood by the players.
this_may_be_it_when: Records released later show a deliberate effort to mislead, which goes beyond a gap in knowledge.
Multiple channels told the same false story, and independent checking shows they traced back to one source.
Something that should have been visible was missing, and something visible was staged.
The people most eager to confirm the story were the ones who gained when you believed it.
Credible historians or investigators have documented the effort with sources, and have not relied on inference alone.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The gap is explained by incomplete information that everyone had.
Independent sources, with different origins, agree on the facts.
The error looks like ordinary analytic bias or wishful thinking.
The party involved has corrected the record when new facts arrived.
The only evidence is that events turned out differently than expected.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Institutions often keep details secret for legitimate security or privacy reasons.
Initial reports in a fast-moving event are often wrong without anyone intending it.
Wrong forecasts usually come from limited information and human error.
common_false_positives: A surprise attack or event that analysts failed to predict. That does not show anyone planned the misdirection.
A company's secret product launch kept under wraps for competitive reasons.
A government that said 'no comment' on an operation.
discernment_questions: Is there documentary evidence that the misleading picture was arranged, or only that I was surprised?
Do my sources really have separate origins, or do they trace back to one?
Who benefits if I believe this account right now?
Would a plain mistake or ordinary secrecy explain this just as well?
What would change my mind, and have I looked for it?
less_concerning_if: The silence has an obvious, stated reason, such as a safety or privacy concern.
Independent reports from different directions line up.
The institution later explains and corrects what it got wrong.
more_concerning_if: Released records show a deliberate plan to mislead.
A suspiciously tidy trail of evidence appears, matching what someone wanted you to conclude.
Those who questioned the story were punished or smeared, not answered.
pattern_over_time_signs: Several stories, from several channels, that all point the same way and prove false together.
A mismatch between official accounts and independent physical or documentary evidence.
Revisions that come only after outside pressure.
Later declassified or leaked records that describe the effort in the institution's own words.
live_fields.repair_check: Once the misleading effort is exposed, accountability looks like release of the underlying records. It also looks like an open correction and a named account of who decided what. It does not look like a new statement that is again careful, partial and impossible to check.
live_fields.boundary_respect_check: When you press for sources, does the account become more checkable, with named documents and independent confirmation? Or does it become more guarded, with you told that doubt itself is unpatriotic or irresponsible?
live_fields.psychological_mechanism: New information is usually read in line with what a person already expects. A picture that matches expectations may be accepted with little checking. Several matching reports look like proof, even when they share one origin. Attention is limited too. What is shown prominently can crowd out what is missing, so the absence goes unnoticed.
live_fields.possible_impact_on_receiver: Readers talk about a gap between the world they thought they understood and what records later showed. Some feel anger or embarrassment at having believed it. After repeated cases, others drift into believing nothing, which leaves them no better equipped. Those who made decisions on the false picture may face real losses.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask for the basis: 'What is the source for this, and has anyone independent confirmed it?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Hold your conclusion open until separate, independent sources agree, and say so if you are asked to take a side.
response_options.disengagement: Step away from fast-moving, unverified claims that ask for an immediate judgment. Return when records or reporting have caught up.
response_options.support_seeking: Discuss what you are seeing with a librarian, a teacher, or an experienced reporter who tracks the topic.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If you analyze, report or decide on such matters, document your sources and how independent they are. Flag the points where one origin sits behind many reports.

live_fields.boundary_script: "Do I know where this actually came from? Are these sources truly separate from each other? Who gains if I believe it, and can I wait for records or independent confirmation before I act?"
live_fields.safety_note: Learning of this kind of effort is rarely a personal danger. It changes if you hold a role where a false picture puts people at risk, such as in emergency, security or journalism work. Raise the concern with a supervisor, an editor or a legal adviser, and keep a record of what you saw.
misuse_warning: Calling every unwelcome fact 'disinformation by design' lets people dismiss inconvenient true information.
Assuming everything official is a staged deception becomes a conspiracy habit, and it is as unreliable as blind trust.
live_fields.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Honey Trapping targets one person through a staged romance. Strategic deception targets what a whole adversary believes. Agent of Influence Operations uses a credible voice to carry a message. Deception concerns the falseness of the picture itself, whoever delivers it. PSYOP Message Framing shapes how people feel about a message. Strategic deception is about hiding what is real and showing a false picture.

Milieu Control.definition: The information and relationships around members are managed by the group, so there is no outside view to check against.

live_fields.expanded_definition: Milieu control means a group manages the information and the relationships around its members. It can be formal, such as banned books or rules about who may be contacted. It can also be informal, such as steady pressure to spend all free time with fellow members. Robert Lifton, who studied thought reform, listed it among the features of totalistic groups. Wanting focus or privacy is normal. It crosses a line once outside contact, news and doubts are discouraged, reported or punished. Then a member has nothing else to test the group's claims against.
live_fields.why_this_matters: Reading, contact and conversation are all bounded by the group. That leaves no outside view to compare anything against, including the question of whether the boundary itself is reasonable.
what_it_is: Rules, spoken or unspoken, about which books, websites, news and media members may use.
Limits on who a member may call, visit or live near, often with family and old friends described as a bad influence.
A calendar so full of meetings, work and service that little time is left for anyone outside.
Members expected to report on each other's contacts, reading or doubts.
Seen in religious groups, political movements, self-improvement programs, communes and close-knit organizations, though most of those do not work this way.
what_it_is_not: Communities of every kind have shared practices, retreats and times of deliberate focus. Choosing to spend most of your time among people who share your commitments is ordinary. The question is whether outside contact and information can resume without penalty.
A silent retreat or monastery that people enter by choice, with a known end date and a way to call home.
A school or workplace that limits phones during working hours.
Parents guiding what a young child watches and reads.
A close family or circle of friends that simply prefers one another's company.
A group that criticizes outside media in the open while members stay free to read it.
this_may_be_it_when: Members who read or contact outsiders have to hide it, or get reported by others.
Former members and relatives are described as enemies, and speaking to them is discouraged.
Outside news reaches members only after leaders have interpreted it.
Phones, mail or travel need permission, and permission is often refused.
A question about the rules draws suspicion about the asker's loyalty.
this_may_not_be_it_when: Members come and go and keep ordinary friendships outside.
Criticism of the group can be read and discussed openly.
A long stretch of time away brings no penalty or interrogation on return.
A restriction has a stated, limited purpose, such as a retreat, and ends when it does.
Relatives are welcome at events and can reach members directly.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: A demanding season, such as a training program or a harvest, can leave little time for friends.
Some faith traditions encourage simple living or limited media, and members choose it gladly.
A new member may drop old habits eagerly, with nobody asking them to.
common_false_positives: A boarding school or military academy with posted phone rules and scheduled family calls.
A group that recommends its own reading list and says other books are welcome too.
A new job or a move that crowds out old routines without anyone intending it.
discernment_questions: Could you contact an old friend or relative tomorrow and speak freely, with nobody asking what was said?
Can you read criticism of the group in full without being asked to justify why?
Does anyone track whom you talk to or what you read?
When you voice a doubt, who finds out about it?
Can you hear from people who left in their own words, or only through the group's description of them?
less_concerning_if: Members can step away for weeks and return to a warm welcome.
Leaders say openly that outside views are fine and members act on it.
Contact limits are short, explained and chosen by the member.
more_concerning_if: Spending time with outsiders brings shaming, extra duties or loss of standing.
Members lack their own money, phone or transport and cannot reach anyone without help from the group.
Members who drift away are cut off from everyone still inside.
pattern_over_time_signs: Your circle of friends outside the group shrinks, one canceled plan at a time.
You stop reading or watching things you used to enjoy without quite deciding to.
You catch yourself describing relatives with the group's words for them.
Doubts feel unsafe to say aloud to anyone, even a person you trust.
live_fields.repair_check: Real change would show as open doors. Contact rules are lifted, outside reading is no longer questioned, and former members are heard directly instead of described. A statement about openness, with the same permission gate still in place, changes nothing a member can feel.
live_fields.boundary_respect_check: Notice what follows an afternoon with an outside friend or an outside article. Curiosity from the group points one way. Questions about who knew, or a cooler reception afterward, point the other.
live_fields.psychological_mechanism: When one group supplies nearly all of a person's information, friendships and daily routine, it can become the standard for what seems normal. Without other voices to compare against, small restrictions tend to feel reasonable, and doubts can start to feel like personal failings. Each step often seems minor on its own.
live_fields.possible_impact_on_receiver: Members report losing touch with friends and family, being unable to judge whether the group's claims hold up, and shame about wanting outside contact. After a long time inside, some say they feel lost in ordinary life, unsure how to rebuild relationships or what to trust.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask a plain question in the group, such as 'Is it all right if I keep up with my sister?' How people receive it tells you a lot.
response_options.firm_boundary: Keep one outside contact steady and ordinary, such as a short weekly call with someone who knew you before, without announcing it. Decide any larger change privately, with a counselor who knows high-control groups.
response_options.disengagement: Take a walk, a nap or a quiet hour alone when pressure builds. Keep one steady contact outside the group informed of how you are.
response_options.support_seeking: Reach someone who knew you before, or a counselor who understands high-control groups, and say what daily life is like in your own words.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a workplace program or training limits contact and outside information, ask for the policy in writing. Keep copies where the organization cannot see them.

live_fields.boundary_script: "Is it all right if I keep up with my sister and my old friends? I'm glad to talk about what the group is doing. I just want to stay in touch with them as well."
live_fields.safety_note: Warning signs include being watched, having your phone, money or documents held, or being told what will happen to people who question. Fear of what follows contact with family is another sign. Decisions about leaving are best made privately, with an experienced advocate, a counselor who knows high-control groups, or a trusted person outside. If you are in immediate danger, contact emergency services.
misuse_warning: Calling a tight-knit congregation, team or family a controlling group because it is close or devout mistakes closeness for control. The test is whether outside contact is penalized.
Telling someone their group is controlling their world can push them to defend it. A question about how free they feel usually lands better than a label.
live_fields.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Doctrine Over Person is about what a member is taught to think of their own experience. Milieu control concerns what reaches them to begin with. Sacred Science makes the doctrine unquestionable. Milieu control makes sure the questions never arrive. Bounded Choice describes how choices come to feel free. Here the matter is simply who may talk to whom.

Demand for Purity.definition: The world is split into pure and corrupt, and members are held to standards no one can meet, so they live in constant failure.

live_fields.expanded_definition: Demand for purity splits the world into the pure and the corrupt. Members are held to near-perfection in thought, speech and behavior. Nobody can meet that, so guilt never ends and the group becomes the only place to find relief. Confession, public correction and watching one another often go with it. Many traditions hold high standards sincerely. This pattern is different because the standard is drawn so that failure is guaranteed and only the group can forgive it.
live_fields.why_this_matters: Nobody can meet the standard, so a person is always a little in the wrong. The only place to find relief is the authority that set the standard.
what_it_is: A sharp line between pure and impure, with members sorted into one or the other.
Standards that cover thoughts, desires and doubts as well as actions.
Rituals of confession or public self-criticism, where lapses are reported to the group.
Shame that is renewed by the rules themselves, since the bar always sits just out of reach.
Relief offered only by the group through its penance, forgiveness or approval.
what_it_is_not: Many traditions and ethical communities hold demanding standards sincerely. Wanting to be better than you are now is not shame-based control. The picture changes when the standard is drawn so that falling short is guaranteed and only the group can forgive it.
A faith's fast, vow or discipline that members choose, with a path back after a lapse.
A recovery program that asks for honest accounting and also offers acceptance after setbacks.
A professional code of conduct that holds people accountable for specific behavior.
Personal conscience. Feeling guilty about something you actually did can be healthy.
A strict family or team culture with high expectations that still lets people fail and be forgiven.
this_may_be_it_when: No one can name a member who has ever fully met the standard.
Private thoughts and doubts are treated as moral failures that must be reported.
Forgiveness is granted only by group leaders, never simply by trying again.
People outside are described as unclean, and contact with them is treated as a lapse.
Members feel more shame the longer they stay.
this_may_not_be_it_when: A lapse is met with support and the person returns to standing at once.
Standards cover chosen actions, not private thoughts.
Members can say they are struggling without being punished or ranked.
The community's ideals are described as aspirations that everyone falls short of together.
Confession, if it exists at all, is optional and kept private.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Ethical traditions often ask for high ideals and honest self-examination, and many people find that meaningful.
New members can feel guilt from their own conscience, not from anyone's pressure.
A leader who is strict about specific safety or conduct rules may simply care about them.
common_false_positives: A religious confession that is voluntary, private and ends with real absolution.
A sports team or military unit with demanding standards of conduct.
A person's own perfectionism, which can exist without any group at all.
discernment_questions: Has anyone you know actually met the standard, and what happened when they did not?
Are your private thoughts treated as something the group has a right to know?
When you fall short, do you feel more shame or more welcome?
Who gets to decide you are forgiven, and can that ever happen without them?
Do you feel clean and light more often now, or heavier?
less_concerning_if: A person who fails is welcomed back without a public process.
Rules concern what people do, and thoughts stay their own.
Members describe the standard as something they chose and can adjust.
more_concerning_if: Confessions are recorded or used later to pressure someone.
Those who admit doubt are shunned, humiliated or made to repeat penance.
Members talk about themselves as worthless or contaminated.
pattern_over_time_signs: The list of things that count as failures gets longer.
You monitor your own thoughts for violations and feel dread when you notice one.
You confess things that once would have seemed too small to mention.
You start to see people outside the group as stained or dangerous.
live_fields.repair_check: Genuine change would mean the standard itself gets looser: penance ends, confessions stay private, and a lapse leaves a person's standing intact. A leader who apologizes for shaming someone while the same impossible measure stays in place has not changed much.
live_fields.boundary_respect_check: Try holding back one private thought and see what happens. If the group accepts that some things are yours, that is a good sign. Pressure to hand it over, or a cooler welcome afterward, says otherwise.
live_fields.psychological_mechanism: Shame often pushes people toward whoever can relieve it. If failure is certain and only the group can forgive, the group can come to feel like the only safe place. When private thoughts count as violations, people may police themselves, so outside control is hardly needed.
live_fields.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe constant guilt, scrupulous checking of their own minds, fear of being found out, and a deep sense of being unclean or unworthy. Some describe feeling lighter after stepping away and then grieving the years spent in that state. Others struggle for a long time to trust their own sense of right and wrong.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask gently about the standard itself: 'Has anyone here ever met this fully? What happens when they don't?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Keep some things private and say so calmly: 'My private thoughts are mine. I'm happy to talk about what I do.'
response_options.disengagement: Sit out a confession or correction session to rest, and spend that time with a person who accepts you as you are.
response_options.support_seeking: Speak with a counselor, therapist or former member who understands shame-based groups. Notice what it is like to be heard without being graded.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a program or workplace requires public confessions or ranks people's character, ask for the policy in writing. You can raise it with an ombudsperson (an independent complaints officer), HR or legal aid.

live_fields.boundary_script: "I take my values seriously, and I'm still going to keep my private thoughts to myself. I can talk about what I do, and I'd like that to be enough."
live_fields.safety_note: Watch for confessions being used as pressure, or shame that turns into thoughts of self-harm. Watch, too, for penances that involve deprivation or pain, or fear of what happens to those who are found impure. If you feel unsafe with yourself, reach a crisis line or emergency services right away. Plans for stepping away are best made privately, with a counselor or advocate who knows high-control groups.
misuse_warning: Calling a faith or ethical community shame-based because its standards are high ignores that many people choose such standards freely. The test is whether failure is guaranteed and only the group can absolve it.
Telling someone their guilt is entirely manufactured can dismiss real conscience about real harm they did.
live_fields.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Sacred Science makes the doctrine unquestionable, while demand for purity makes you unworthy by its measure. Doctrine Over Person says your experience is wrong, while this says your self is stained. Dispensing of Existence ranks people by worth and treats outsiders as lesser. This one keeps insiders permanently short of the standard.

Thought Control.made_of: Loaded Language + Thought-Stopping Clichés + Sacred Science + Doctrine Over Person + Phobia Indoctrination
Thought Control.definition: Control of language, interpretation, and critical analysis.

live_fields.expanded_definition: Thought control works on the vocabulary a person uses to think. Instead of arguing one point, a group or relationship supplies loaded terms for insiders and outsiders. It treats questions as signs of a problem in the asker, and offers a single explanation for any doubt. Every community has shorthand, and strong belief is not control. What matters is whether disagreement can be voiced without being relabeled, whether outside sources may be read, and whether leaving is possible. It is judged by those conditions, never by whether the belief itself is true.
live_fields.why_this_matters: The words you would use to examine the situation are supplied from inside it, so doubt arrives already labeled as a symptom. Questions that cannot be asked cannot be answered, and you may lose a way to check your own thinking.
what_it_is: A private vocabulary that has a label, such as 'worldly' or 'deceived', for people who leave or object, and the label ends the discussion.
Questions treated as evidence of a problem in the person asking, instead of as questions.
One explanation offered for every kind of doubt, whatever the doubt was about.
Found in high-control groups, in some families and workplaces, and in online communities with strict insider language.
Judged by openness and not by what is believed. That means whether outside information may be read and disagreement heard.
what_it_is_not: Shared shorthand, which every family, profession and fan community develops over time. It is normal and does not control anyone.
A belief you hold independently and can explain in your own words, including to someone who disagrees.
Passionate, sincere conviction, which is different from a mechanism that suppresses dissent.
A teacher or coach insisting on one method for a while so you can learn it, while you stay free to question it afterwards.
Someone disagreeing with you firmly and giving reasons, which is argument and not control.
A religious or political community with strong norms that welcomes questions and lets people leave without penalty.
this_may_be_it_when: Questions get a label instead of an answer.
The same short explanation is given for every doubt.
Outside books, friends or news are described as contaminating.
People who left are described in fixed terms, and talking to them is discouraged.
You notice yourself using the group's phrases for your own feelings and cannot find other words.
this_may_not_be_it_when: People can explain the beliefs in their own words and differ from one another.
Hard questions are answered, or admitted to be hard.
Outside reading and friendships are fine.
People who left are still spoken of with respect and stay in touch.
The shared phrases are a convenience that people drop easily when talking to outsiders.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Specialist groups develop jargon that makes talk quicker, such as nurses, programmers or climbers.
Someone newly drawn to a view may sound repetitive while still learning it.
A close family can have private sayings that nobody feels trapped by.
common_false_positives: A team using acronyms that confuse newcomers.
A new believer who repeats a leader's phrases with enthusiasm and yet remains free to question.
A strict training program with a defined end and an open exit.
discernment_questions: Can I explain what I believe without borrowing the group's phrases?
When I raise a doubt, do I get an answer or a label?
Am I allowed to read or hear the other side?
How are people who left described, and could I talk with them?
If I changed my mind, what would it cost me?
less_concerning_if: Doubts are met with reasons and not with labels.
Members hold different views and still belong.
Contact with outsiders is welcome and not policed.
more_concerning_if: Questioning is treated as proof of weakness, outside influence or disloyalty.
Contact with outsiders or with people who left is discouraged or forbidden.
Changing your mind would cost you housing, income, family or community.
pattern_over_time_signs: Your own vocabulary shrinks, and your explanations become the group's.
Doubts get rehearsed in private and then dropped.
Old friends find you harder to talk with, because your words have changed.
You begin labeling other people's questions the way yours were labeled.
live_fields.repair_check: Real change would let a doubt be stated plainly and answered on its merits. Outside sources would be welcome, and no label would be put on the person who asked. Kind words that keep the same labels for disagreement leave the structure untouched.
live_fields.boundary_respect_check: Ask one plain question, such as where a claim comes from, and see how the conversation goes. An open reply names sources and tolerates 'I'm not sure yet'. A reply that questions your loyalty, state of mind or commitment treats the question itself as the problem.
live_fields.psychological_mechanism: Thinking happens in whatever words are available. If a framework supplies the only words for a doubt, such as 'weakness' or 'attack', the doubt may look like evidence against yourself. Belonging, approval and meaning are often at stake. That makes agreeing rewarding and questioning costly, until checking things independently starts to seem unsafe or disloyal.
live_fields.possible_impact_on_receiver: Some report an inner censor that stops a thought before it forms, or find that their own words for feelings have faded. Others describe relief on meeting outside language that fits their experience, along with grief and anger. Contact with old friends can feel strange once the shared vocabulary is gone.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask a curious, narrow question and note the answer: 'Where does that come from? I'd like to read it myself.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Hold your ground quietly with 'I'm going to think about that before I agree,' and repeat it as often as needed. Do not argue the point.
response_options.disengagement: Keep your words few and neutral in heated debates, and use the time between sessions to read, walk and talk with people outside.
response_options.support_seeking: Find someone outside who is not part of the group, such as a counselor experienced with high-control groups or a friend from before, and describe specific phrases and what happened when you questioned them.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: In a workplace with enforced slogans, keep a record of meetings where questions were answered with labels. Bring your concerns to HR or an employee representative in writing.

live_fields.boundary_script: "This is still sinking in for me, and a bit more reading would help before I decide. Where does that come from?"
live_fields.safety_note: Danger signals include being cut off from outside contacts, and risking housing, income or children for disagreeing. Others are being told that going elsewhere means ruin, or being watched for doubt. Keep your questions low-key and your plans to yourself. Contact a counselor experienced with high-control groups, or legal aid if custody or housing is at stake. Work out any next step privately with them.
misuse_warning: If you call any community with its own vocabulary 'thought control', you dismiss members who are there freely and are glad to be.
The label describes how doubt is handled, so it should not be used to mean that a belief is false.
live_fields.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Loyalty Binds makes silence the price of belonging. Thought control supplies the vocabulary that makes questions sound like symptoms. Self-Gaslighting Induction is doubting your memory of events. Here the doubt is over whether you may think a thought at all. Learned Helplessness tells you that you cannot cope alone, while thought control tells you that your own reading cannot be trusted.

Dark Patterns (AI-Adaptive).made_of: Manufactured Urgency + Manufactured Scarcity + Buried Consent + Gamified Compulsion + Algorithmic Manipulation
Dark Patterns (AI-Adaptive).definition: Screens are built so the quickest or most visible path is the one that serves the platform, and the design adjusts to what works on you.

live_fields.expanded_definition: Dark patterns are screens built so the quickest path is not the one a person would pick with time to read. Examples are a hidden decline button, a pre-checked box, a countdown timer, or a cancel flow that takes ten steps. The AI-adaptive version changes the screen for each user, based on what the system has learned about them. Good design nudges too, and a confusing checkout is usually just badly built. The concern is design that gets harder to escape the more it learns.
live_fields.why_this_matters: Money, personal data and consent leave a person's hands through interfaces built so the default path is not what they would have chosen. People often blame themselves for clicking, when the screen was arranged to produce the click.
what_it_is: Screens that make one choice easy and bright and the other small, hidden or phrased as a loss.
Subscription traps: signing up takes one tap and canceling takes a maze of pages or a phone call.
Consent boxes that are pre-checked, or whose decline option is worded to make you feel foolish.
Pressure cues such as countdown clocks or 'only 2 left' notices that may or may not be true.
In the AI-adaptive form, the layout, timing or message changes between users. The system predicts what will work on each of them.
what_it_is_not: A prominent save button or a sensible default is ordinary design. It helps people finish what they came to do.
A confusing checkout is much more often badly built or hurried than built to work against you.
A real limited-time sale or truly low stock. Scarcity messages can be accurate.
A retention offer that appears once and then lets you cancel without further obstacle.
A business making its preferred option more prominent while keeping the other one clear and easy.
What separates this from ordinary clutter is an interface that gets harder to escape the more it learns about one user.
this_may_be_it_when: Leaving, declining or canceling is much harder than signing up, with no practical reason.
The wording of the decline option is built to shame or confuse you.
Urgency notices change or vanish when you wait or reload.
Two people see noticeably different prices, offers or pressure for the same product.
Settings that protect your data are hidden several screens deep or switch back on after updates.
this_may_not_be_it_when: Everyone sees the same screen, and canceling takes about as many steps as signing up.
The extra step is a real safeguard, such as confirming a deletion that cannot be undone.
The timer or stock count is accurate and shown to everyone.
The page is simply cluttered, old or poorly translated.
You skipped reading the options on a screen that was fairly laid out.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: A rushed or outdated site where design shortcuts pile up without anyone planning them.
A company testing which layout converts best, which is common and not always aimed at undermining choice.
A cancellation step that exists to prevent accidental loss of an account.
common_false_positives: Prices that differ because of region, tax, shipping or sign-in status.
A real stock shortage presented as 'only 2 left'.
A privacy prompt that is clear but repeated on each new device.
discernment_questions: Are the accept and decline options equally easy to see and equally easy to tap?
Could I leave this service as quickly as I joined it?
Would a different person with the same screen see the same offers and warnings?
Is the urgency real, or does it reset when I come back?
Did the screen tell me plainly what I was agreeing to, or did I have to hunt for it?
less_concerning_if: Both choices are shown clearly, in the same style, with honest wording.
You can cancel in the same place and with about the same effort as signing up.
Terms and total price are stated before you commit.
more_concerning_if: The service targets people the system has flagged as stressed, lonely, in debt or young.
Charges continue after you believe you canceled.
Data or permissions are taken that the service does not need to work.
pattern_over_time_signs: You find charges for services you never meant to keep.
Privacy settings you turned off are back on after an update.
Each time you try to leave, a new obstacle or offer appears.
You spend more on the app during low moments, and the app's prompts seem to arrive at those moments.
live_fields.repair_check: When a company fixes this properly, the refund arrives without a fight and the cancel path becomes short and plain. The screen changes for everyone. A new apology banner over the same maze is not a fix. Neither is a refund only for those who complain loudly.
live_fields.boundary_respect_check: A fair test is whether your 'no' holds. After you decline an option, does it stay declined, or does the same request return next session in new wording? A choice that keeps being re-asked was never being treated as a choice.
live_fields.psychological_mechanism: People who are under time pressure, tired or distracted often take the path that looks default or bright. They also avoid effort that looks like it will be a fight. Screens that put friction on one choice and not the other can use this. When the system also adjusts to a person's habits or low moments, the pressure can land more precisely than a fixed design would.
live_fields.possible_impact_on_receiver: Reports include surprise charges, finding subscriptions they forgot, feeling foolish for clicking, and tiredness from fighting cancellation flows. Some give up on privacy settings because they keep resetting. Others say they trust no checkout screen afterward, and read every box with suspicion.

response_options.soft_clarification: Contact the company in writing. Say exactly what you believed you agreed to and what you were charged, and ask for a correction.
response_options.firm_boundary: On each screen, decline the optional add-ons and data permissions. Keep a screenshot of the final confirmation before you pay.
response_options.disengagement: Close the page when the pressure cue appears and come back later. Check the same offer on another device before committing.
response_options.support_seeking: If a charge will not reverse, contact your card issuer or bank. You could also try a consumer protection office or a local consumer advocate.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If you work in product or design, flag screens where the decline path is harder than the accept path. Use your organization's review or ethics process.

live_fields.boundary_script: "I did not set out to buy this or share that. Before I tap anything, is the 'no' option as easy to find as the 'yes', and would I choose this if there were no clock on it?"
live_fields.safety_note: This is mainly a consumer harm, but it becomes more serious when it takes money from someone who cannot afford it or targets children. It also does when it collects location or contact data that could be used against them. Gather statements and screenshots, contact your bank or card issuer, and ask a consumer advocate or legal aid for help.
misuse_warning: Calling every upsell a dark pattern is unfair to honest businesses. They simply want to sell something and show the options clearly.
Blaming people who clicked can hide the fact that a screen was arranged to produce that click.
live_fields.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Algorithmic Manipulation acts through what a feed shows over weeks. A dark pattern works at the point of a specific decision, such as a button or a form. AI-Driven Social Engineering impersonates someone to get you to act. Dark patterns come from the real service you are already using. Parasocial Manipulation Engineering builds a felt relationship, but a dark pattern needs no relationship at all, only a screen built to win the click.

Pig Butchering (Long-Con Digital Fraud).made_of: Social Engineering -> Manufactured Intimacy -> Future Faking -> Bait and Switch -> Manufactured Urgency
Pig Butchering (Long-Con Digital Fraud).definition: A long, warm online relationship builds trust over weeks or months before you are steered into a fake investment or a request for money.

live_fields.expanded_definition: The name comes from the idea of fattening an animal before slaughter. It describes a fraud that unfolds slowly. It often begins with a wrong-number text or a friendly message. It grows into a daily friendship or romance. Only later does it turn to money, usually a trading or crypto platform that looks real and even shows gains. One friendly stranger is common and mostly harmless. What stands out is a relationship that never asks for anything until it introduces a platform. Then it keeps raising the stakes.
live_fields.why_this_matters: After months of unhurried, ordinary relationship-building, the request finally comes from someone you have real reason to trust. The losses can be life-changing, and shame often keeps people from telling anyone until the money is gone.
what_it_is: A first contact that starts by chance, such as a message to a wrong number or a friendly follow, and turns into daily conversation.
A warm relationship, romantic or friendly, in which the other person seems to share your life and values.
Money entering the picture only later, through an investment or trading platform the new friend recommends.
