A site or app that shows impressive gains but makes withdrawals difficult or always one payment away.
A scheme run by organized groups with many victims in the pipeline, and not a lone person making it up as they go.
what_it_is_not: Real friendships and relationships do begin online and build slowly. Someone talking happily about their own investments may simply be doing that. The turn to notice is a relationship that has asked for nothing starting to steer money toward a platform it introduced.
A real wrong-number text where both people say sorry and move on.
A friend recommending an investment they honestly use, who is easy to verify and does not push.
A long-distance relationship with video calls, mutual friends and no money requests.
A legitimate investment platform with a known, registered operator and normal withdrawals.
this_may_be_it_when: A stranger who contacted you first steers the conversation to money or an investment platform.
They avoid live video, in-person meetings or anything that can be independently verified.
The platform is reached by a link they supply and is not one you can check through independent sources.
Withdrawals are blocked by new fees, taxes or minimum deposits.
You are told to keep it secret, or you feel nudged away from asking family or a financial professional.
this_may_not_be_it_when: You can meet or video-call them live, and they have a verifiable life with real mutual contacts.
They never ask for money or investment participation, and take no offense at your caution.
Any platform mentioned is one you found on your own and can check with a regulator.
Withdrawals work cleanly in any amount at any time.
They are glad for you to talk over any financial decision with other people.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Wrong-number messages happen innocently, and many lead to nothing more than a polite exchange.
People who are shy on camera or travel a lot may be slow to video-call for ordinary reasons.
Friends honestly share that they invest and what they use, without a script.
common_false_positives: An online friend who talks about their own crypto holdings but never pushes yours.
A new romance with a slow, ordinary pace of getting to know someone.
A genuine investment club or advisor who is licensed, transparent and pressure-free.
discernment_questions: Have I met this person live on video, and could someone else confirm they exist?
Who contacted whom first, and how did money enter the conversation?
Can I confirm the platform with an independent regulator, and not through links they sent?
Is anything stopping me from taking my money out today?
Would I be comfortable showing this whole conversation to a family member or my bank?
less_concerning_if: The relationship has stayed free of money talk and has real-world anchors.
Any investment idea was yours, researched independently, and on a regulated platform.
You told someone you trust about it and they were not worried after hearing everything.
more_concerning_if: You have already sent money, or borrowed or cashed out savings to deposit more.
You are being told to hurry, keep it secret, or pay a fee to release your own funds.
You are lonely, grieving or newly separated, when the relationship feels like a lifeline.
pattern_over_time_signs: Contact is constant, daily and affectionate, and it always seems to arrive just as you feel low.
The topic of money, success or a lucky opportunity appears more and more often.
Your deposits grow while your ability to withdraw shrinks.
You find yourself hiding the relationship or the investment from people close to you.
live_fields.repair_check: If a person or platform were genuine, you could take all your money out without a new fee. You could also check who runs it, and talk to anyone you like. A delay, a surprise charge or an appeal to your trust in them is not repair.
live_fields.boundary_respect_check: What happens when you say you want to pause, ask a professional, or withdraw? Someone with your interests at heart is comfortable with all three. Hurt feelings, a deadline or a sudden obstacle to leaving suggests your caution is being treated as the thing to overcome.
live_fields.psychological_mechanism: Steady attention and affection over weeks can build real trust and attachment. People may feel they owe something to, or want to protect, a relationship they value. Early small gains on a platform may look like proof. Once money is in, people often want not to lose it and feel shame at admitting a mistake. That can push them to deposit more and tell fewer people. Loneliness deepens the pull.
live_fields.possible_impact_on_receiver: Many lose savings, retirement money or borrowed funds. Some grieve for a relationship that turned out not to be what it seemed, and carry deep shame that kept them silent. Others describe sleeplessness, strained family ties and trouble trusting new people afterward. Many also feel relief on learning that skilled, organized fraud was involved, and not personal failure.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask to meet on live video now. Say you would like to talk the idea over with a family member or advisor before any money moves. Then notice whether that is welcomed.
response_options.firm_boundary: Do not send further money, crypto or fees. Do not move funds on instructions from someone you have not met in person, however convincing the dashboard looks.
response_options.disengagement: Stop replying. Keep the messages and screenshots instead of deleting them, and avoid answering later contacts who offer to recover your funds for a fee.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell someone you trust today. Contact your bank or card provider, and report it to your national fraud-reporting service and local police. Ask a consumer-protection or victim-support organization what to do next.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If you work in banking, a platform or customer support, flag unusual large transfers to new crypto or trading sites. Pay extra attention to customers who mention an online friend. Follow your fraud-escalation process.

live_fields.boundary_script: "I've decided not to move any money until a trusted person and my bank have looked at all of this. I also want to check the platform through a regulator on my own. If it's real, it will hold up to that."
live_fields.safety_note: This is financial entrapment that can wipe out savings and sometimes pushes people into debt, lost housing or despair. Warning signs are pressure to borrow or cash out retirement funds, secrecy and fee demands to release your money. Contact your bank right away, report it, and reach out to victim support or legal aid. If you feel hopeless, talk to someone now or call a crisis line.
misuse_warning: Without evidence, telling a friend their new online romance must be a scam can damage a real relationship. It can also push them away from you.
Blaming victims as gullible adds shame to loss and keeps people from reporting, which is exactly what the fraud relies on.
live_fields.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Parasocial Manipulation Engineering uses a one-sided bond with an audience figure. Here the bond is a personal, seemingly two-way friendship or romance aimed at one victim. Synthetic Persona Networks may supply the fake faces and voices. This tactic is defined by the slow path from trust to a money request. Dark Patterns (AI-Adaptive) trick a click in an interface, and here the trick is the relationship itself.

Trauma Bonding.definition: The attachment formed through cycles of harm and relief that draws you back.

live_fields.expanded_definition: Trauma bonding is an attachment that grows in a relationship where harm and relief come from the same source. After a frightening or painful episode, the person who caused it is also the one who apologizes, soothes or becomes tender. That comfort can feel unusually intense. Ordinary couples fight and make up, so a single quarrel is not this. The pattern is a repeating cycle, where the closeness after the pain is taken as proof of how deep the bond is.
live_fields.why_this_matters: Relief and harm come from the same person. So your strongest feeling of closeness can arrive just after the worst treatment, and then become a reason to stay. Knowing this can help you tell the strength of a feeling from the safety of a relationship.
what_it_is: A cycle where a hurtful episode is followed by apology, tenderness, gifts or a heartfelt reunion from the person who caused it.
A bond that feels stronger after the worst episodes than it did before them.
A relationship where the comforter and the source of fear are one person, so there is nowhere else to turn for relief.
A shared sense that 'what we go through together proves our love', which makes the harm part of the story of the bond.
what_it_is_not: Two people bonded by shared hardship from outside, such as caring for a sick child or surviving a disaster. Neither is the source of the pain.
A couple who quarrel loudly, apologize honestly and change something afterwards, so the same fight does not repeat.
Ordinary attachment to someone you love who hurt you once and has since taken full responsibility.
The strong loyalty of family members who have been through difficult years together, with no one inflicting the harm.
A person's long-standing attachment style, which may make partings painful without anyone causing the pain.
this_may_be_it_when: The reconciliations after bad episodes feel like the most intense moments of the relationship.
You find yourself defending the person to friends while also being afraid of them.
The same kind of harm returns, and the same kind of comfort follows it.
Leaving brings a sharp physical longing, even though you know how things have been.
The person who hurt you is the only one you want when you are upset.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The hard moments are honestly acknowledged and the behavior changes afterwards.
Comfort and support come from several people besides the one involved in the conflict.
The hurtful incidents were few, real repair followed, and months have passed without a repeat.
Your feelings of closeness are steady and do not spike after conflict.
You feel free to leave a conversation or a room without being afraid of what follows.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Many people feel unusually close after an emotional reconciliation, even in healthy relationships, because strong feelings are being shared.
Grief and shared loss can bring people together in a way that feels intense and is not harmful.
Staying through a hard stretch can come from loyalty, love and practical limits such as money or children. It does not have to come from a bond to the harm.
common_false_positives: A couple in counseling who feel raw and close after an honest session about a real problem.
Soldiers, nurses or siblings who bonded through a shared ordeal.
A single serious argument, followed by sincere change, that left the relationship stronger.
discernment_questions: Do I feel closest to this person right after they have hurt me?
Is the person who comforts me the same person who caused the distress?
Has this cycle of harm and reconciliation happened more than a couple of times?
When I tell friends the good parts, do I leave out the other parts?
If someone I loved described this relationship, how worried would I be?
less_concerning_if: Harm has stopped, and the closeness has remained steady without needing a crisis.
You have other people you turn to for comfort, and you do turn to them.
The person has acknowledged specific hurts and shown lasting change.
more_concerning_if: The harm includes fear for your physical safety, threats, or humiliation in front of others.
Reconciliation follows each episode quickly and keeps you from speaking to anyone else.
You cannot picture life without the person, and the prospect of leaving brings panic.
pattern_over_time_signs: Each cycle seems to cost a bit more, and the make-up comes with higher stakes or bigger gestures.
You pull away from people who express concern, because they do not seem to see the good side.
You have left or tried to leave more than once and returned during a warm period.
Your idea of what counts as a normal bad day has shifted over time.
live_fields.repair_check: Real change here is dull and visible. The harmful episodes stop altogether, and closeness no longer depends on a crisis first. Intense reconciliation scenes after each new incident, with the behavior underneath unchanged, are the cycle itself and not the end of it.
live_fields.boundary_respect_check: Consider what the apology is asked to do. When you say you need the harmful behavior to stop, is the answer a different way of acting? Or is it another emotional reunion that leaves you grateful and quiet? The second keeps the loop closed.
live_fields.psychological_mechanism: Fear and distress can heighten the need for comfort. If comfort is available from only one person, attachment to them may deepen. Relief after a threat can feel especially strong and can be mistaken for love. Cut off from other support, a person may find it harder to see the cycle. The strength of the feeling may even seem to prove the relationship is right.
live_fields.possible_impact_on_receiver: Reported experiences include being torn between dread and longing, and shame about missing the person who hurt you. People also report being unable to explain to others why you stay. Some say they felt addicted to the reconciliation. Many describe a long period after leaving when the pull stayed strong. This surprised them, and they took it, wrongly, as a sign that leaving was a mistake.

response_options.soft_clarification: If it is safe to speak, name the cycle in one sentence: 'I notice we are closest right after we have hurt each other. I want closeness without the hurt first.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Decide privately, with an advocate and not with the other person, what you would do if it happened again. Announcing a deadline or a consequence to someone who may react badly can raise the risk. Keep that plan to yourself and the people helping you.
response_options.disengagement: Plan any exit with care: gather documents, pick a safe place to go, and tell someone beforehand. Expect the pull to be strongest in the first weeks.
response_options.support_seeking: Talk on your own, not as a couple, to a counselor or advocate trained in relationship harm. Also keep up contact with at least one person outside the relationship who knows the whole story.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: A boss, teacher or mentor may alternate harsh treatment with warmth, leaving you feeling tied to them. If so, speak to HR, an ombudsperson (an independent complaints officer) or a mentor elsewhere. Do this before the next cycle.

live_fields.boundary_script: "I know you're sorry, and I can tell how much you mean it right now. What I need is for the apology to be followed by something different. Can we pause here for tonight? I'd like some quiet time to think about how these cycles go."
live_fields.safety_note: This pattern can come with physical violence, threats, stalking, and control over money or contact. The days around leaving are often the riskiest. Watch for escalation, strangulation, threats to kill or to harm children or pets, and weapons. Ask a domestic violence advocate to help you build a leaving plan. It can include where your documents, a spare phone and a go-bag will be kept.
misuse_warning: Telling someone in a hard relationship that they are 'just trauma bonded' can dismiss their real love, real reasons and practical constraints. It can also push them away.
Using the term for any intense make-up after a quarrel mislabels ordinary couple life as something sinister.
live_fields.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Kindness placed right after harm, to reset what you will tolerate, is the move called Relief Bait. Trauma bonding is the attachment that can result when this is repeated. Intermittent Reinforcement concerns the unpredictable timing of rewards, whether or not pain precedes them. Conditional Love sets out terms; here the terms are never stated, and the bond is felt as love.

Idealize-Devalue-Discard Cycle.made_of: Love Bombing -> Pedestal Ploy -> Contempt -> Sudden Devaluation
Idealize-Devalue-Discard Cycle.definition: The full arc of elevation, destruction, and disposal.

live_fields.expanded_definition: This describes a whole relationship arc. It starts with a dazzling stretch in which you feel uniquely seen. Then comes a gradual turn in which the same qualities are criticized. It ends in a way that can feel abrupt or cold. Many relationships cool from early infatuation, and that alone is not this. What marks it is a turn that is sharp and out of proportion to anything you did. The criticism targets what was praised before, and people who knew the person describe the same arc with others.
live_fields.why_this_matters: You measure the ending against the extraordinary beginning and conclude you must have caused the decline. That same conclusion keeps you trying to earn the beginning back. It can be hard to grieve a relationship that changed shape so completely.
what_it_is: An opening stretch of intense admiration, fast closeness and big statements about how special you are.
A middle phase in which the same traits that were praised become faults, and comparisons or small cruelties appear.
An ending that can be sudden, cold, or carried out by silence, often with little explanation.
A sequence that some people report seeing repeat across several relationships, with similar language each time.
what_it_is_not: The normal end of infatuation, where the first intensity settles into something calmer and both people are still kind.
A relationship that ended because of real, specific problems both people could name, such as different wants about children or place.
Disappointment that goes both ways, with each person feeling let down and able to say why.
One painful break-up after a fast start, with no sign of the same arc elsewhere in the person's history.
A person ending a relationship plainly and respectfully, even if the way it ended hurts.
this_may_be_it_when: The early praise was extreme and fast, and it now reads as a script you were handed.
The turn does not follow any event, and the criticism seems to be about who you are.
Qualities they loved are now listed as flaws.
You are compared with a partner they once idealized in the same words.
The end arrives with little discussion, such as being blocked or ghosted.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The cooling follows a specific, nameable event that either of you could discuss.
They still show care and respect while saying the relationship isn't working.
You can both describe what changed, and the descriptions roughly match.
Their past relationships ended for varied reasons with no repeated arc.
The ending came with a conversation, even a hard one.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People often idealize a new partner and later see them more realistically. That can bring a sense of loss without being a tactic.
A person who is anxious about commitment may pull away once things get serious.
Early excitement can fade when people discover real differences. The ending can be clumsy rather than cruel.
common_false_positives: A whirlwind romance that cooled into a more ordinary one and then ended by mutual agreement.
A friendship that was close for a season and drifted apart as lives changed.
A bad break-up in which both people said unkind things at the end.
discernment_questions: Did the praise at the start feel unusually big and fast, and the criticism unusually sharp?
Can I name an event that changed things, or did the shift seem to come from nowhere?
Do the qualities they now criticize match the ones they once loved?
What do people who knew them before say about their earlier relationships?
Did the ending allow any conversation, or was I cut off?
less_concerning_if: Both of you can describe the relationship's rise and decline in similar terms.
The criticism is specific and about behavior, not about your worth.
more_concerning_if: The criticism is public, or directed at you in front of others, or shared with mutual friends.
A new person is already being praised in the same words before the old relationship is over.
The discard comes with retaliation, such as smearing you or withholding shared property.
pattern_over_time_signs: You find yourself trying to be again the person they first described.
Their stories of former partners all follow the same shape: wonderful, then disappointing.
Your confidence drops as the criticism grows, and you hold on to memories of the start.
After the end, you replay the beginning and wonder what you did to lose it.
live_fields.repair_check: Real change would show in how they talk about the whole arc. They would recognize that the early praise was larger than any person could live up to, and that the criticism was out of proportion. A return to warmth with a fresh round of praise starts the first stage again.
live_fields.boundary_respect_check: Ask them to speak about specific behavior instead of general character. Notice whether they can name what happened and keep that frame. Or does the criticism widen into your whole personality, with the praise from the start quoted back as evidence of how you fell?
live_fields.psychological_mechanism: Being idealized can feel intoxicating, and a person may build part of their sense of self on it. When treatment then turns, the contrast with the early warmth often sends people searching for what they did wrong. They try to recover the start. Because the beginning was real to them, they may remain hopeful long after the relationship has changed.
live_fields.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe whiplash, and grief for a version of the relationship that may never have been stable. They also doubt their own judgment about who to trust. Some say they felt discarded as if they were an object. Others describe an urge to explain themselves to the other person long after contact had ended. They wanted to restore the early view.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask about the change directly: 'You used to say you loved how driven I am. Now it sounds like a flaw. What changed for you?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Refuse the rewrite: 'I won't agree that I am a different person from the one you praised. If there is a problem with something I did, tell me what it was.'
response_options.disengagement: Resist the urge to win the early version back. Stop auditioning, keep your own routine, and let distance show whether the respect is still there.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell a friend the whole arc in order, including the early praise and the later criticism. Ask them what they noticed at each stage. Grief counseling can also help with the loss of the idealized start.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a boss or mentor praises you extravagantly and then freezes you out, keep dated records of your work and their feedback. Talk to HR or a mentor outside the relationship.

live_fields.boundary_script: "I was happy when you thought so highly of me, and I'm not the same person you're describing now. If you're unhappy with something I did, tell me what it was. I won't accept being told I was never who you thought I was."
live_fields.safety_note: The arc itself is an emotional harm, not a physical one. It becomes more serious if the discard comes with a smear campaign, stalking or threats. It also does if you suddenly lose housing or income because you shared a home or business. If that begins, keep dated copies of messages and lock down your accounts. Talk to a lawyer or a domestic abuse advocate about protecting your housing and finances.
misuse_warning: Using the label for anyone who ended a relationship after an intense beginning treats ordinary heartbreak as proof of a pattern.
Describing a former partner in these terms to friends can become a smear of its own, built from one side of the story.
live_fields.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Love Bombing covers only the first stage, the overwhelming early affection, and can happen without the later criticism. Hoovering comes after the ending, when the person reappears to pull you back. Negging is a steady stream of backhanded put-downs that can occur at any point. The cycle is the whole three-part arc, from the pedestal through the decline to the drop.
